cls: Anticonvulsant - barbiturate analogue (metabolized to phenobarbital and PEMA)
quick: Maintenance 250 mg orally three to four times daily (250 mg t.i.d.-q.i.d.); titrate up from 100-125 mg at bedtime
May be taken with or without food
Risk of fetal harm; enroll in NAAED Pregnancy Registry (1-888-233-2334). Do not stop abruptly
Appears in milk in substantial quantities; watch infant for somnolence/drowsiness - discontinue nursing if it occurs
Use with caution; primidone and metabolites are renally cleared - reduce frequency in impairment
Use with caution; metabolized in liver to phenobarbital and PEMA
Avoid - additive CNS depression and sedation
Mood/suicidality and sedation; CBC and SMA-12 every 6 months; serum level 5-12 mcg/mL
summary: Primidone is an anticonvulsant used alone or with other agents to control grand mal, psychomotor, and focal seizures, including grand mal refractory to other therapy. It is metabolized to phenobarbital and phenylethylmalonamide (PEMA), both active anticonvulsants. Marked sedation, drowsiness, and ataxia are common early in therapy, and - as with all antiepileptic drugs - it carries a class risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior. Abrupt withdrawal can precipitate status epilepticus.
indications: Control of grand mal (generalized tonic-clonic) seizures
May control grand mal seizures refractory to other anticonvulsant therapy

dosage.d: Days 1-3: 100-125 mg at bedtime; Days 4-6: 100-125 mg twice daily; Days 7-9: 100-125 mg three times daily
dosage.n: Use 50 mg or scored 250 mg tablets; advance toward maintenance on day 10

dosage.d: Day 10 onward: 250 mg three times daily; usual maintenance 750-1000 mg/day in divided doses
dosage.n: May increase to 1250-1500 mg/day if needed; do not exceed 500 mg q.i.d. (2 g/day max)

dosage.c: Epilepsy - patients already on other anticonvulsants
dosage.d: Start 100-125 mg at bedtime; increase gradually to maintenance while tapering the other drug
dosage.n: Transition to primidone monotherapy should take at least 2 weeks

dosage.d: Days 1-3: 50 mg at bedtime; Days 4-6: 50 mg twice daily; Days 7-9: 100 mg twice daily; Day 10 onward: 125 mg three times daily up to 250 mg three times daily
dosage.n: Usual maintenance 125-250 mg three times daily, or 10-25 mg/kg/day in divided doses

admin: Titrate gradually using the stepwise bedtime-then-divided-dose schedule to limit early ataxia/sedation
Take divided doses through the day; the bedtime dose helps reduce daytime drowsiness during titration
Do not stop abruptly - abrupt withdrawal may precipitate status epilepticus; taper under supervision
Allow several weeks to assess efficacy of a given regimen
Serum level determination (target 5-12 mcg/mL) may guide adjustment in select patients
moa: Primidone raises the seizure threshold and alters seizure patterns; the exact mechanism is not fully established. It is metabolized to two active anticonvulsant metabolites - phenobarbital and phenylethylmalonamide (PEMA). Phenobarbital potentiates GABA-mediated inhibition by prolonging chloride channel opening, contributing to the overall anticonvulsant effect.

relative: History of depression or suicidal ideation (AED class risk)
Aspirin/tartrazine sensitivity (250 mg tablet contains FD&C Yellow No. 5)
monitor: Mood, depression, and suicidal thoughts or behavior
CBC and SMA-12 (every 6 months on prolonged therapy)

preg: Effects in human pregnancy are not fully known; anticonvulsant use in women with epilepsy is associated with an elevated incidence of birth defects. Do not discontinue abruptly, as seizures may harm both mother and fetus. Advise pregnant patients to enroll in the North American Antiepileptic Drug (NAAED) Pregnancy Registry (1-888-233-2334).
lact: Primidone appears in breast milk in substantial quantities. Undue somnolence and drowsiness in a nursing newborn should be taken as an indication to discontinue nursing.
renal: Primidone and its metabolites (phenobarbital, PEMA) are renally eliminated. Use with caution and consider reduced dose/extended interval in renal impairment to avoid accumulation and excess sedation.
hepatic: Metabolized in the liver to phenobarbital and PEMA. Use with caution in hepatic impairment; impaired metabolism may alter metabolite levels and increase sedation.

major: Other CNS depressants and sedatives (additive sedation/respiratory depression)
Other antiepileptics - abrupt change in any agent risks status epilepticus
moderate: As a phenobarbital precursor, induces hepatic enzymes and may lower levels of many co-administered drugs
Oral contraceptives (reduced efficacy via enzyme induction)
minor: Folic acid - megaloblastic anemia from primidone responds to folic acid
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - additive CNS depression and sedation
interactions.diagnostics: May warrant periodic CBC and SMA-12; therapeutic serum level 5-12 mcg/mL

serious: Suicidal thoughts or behavior (antiepileptic class risk - monitor for new/worsening depression or mood change)
Marked sedation, drowsiness, and ataxia - especially early in therapy
rare: Megaloblastic anemia (idiosyncratic; responds to folic acid)
Allergic-type reactions to FD&C Yellow No. 5 (tartrazine) in the 250 mg tablet
emergency: Emergence or worsening of suicidal ideation/behavior - seek help immediately
Signs of severe blood dyscrasia (fever, sore throat, unexplained bruising/bleeding)

monitoring: Mood, depression, and suicidal thoughts or behavior - throughout therapy, including early after starting
Sedation, drowsiness, and ataxia - particularly early in therapy
Complete blood count and SMA-12 every 6 months on prolonged therapy
Serum primidone level (therapeutic range 5-12 mcg/mL) when optimizing dose
counsel: Antiepileptic drugs, including primidone, can increase the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior - watch for new or worsening depression, mood changes, or thoughts of self-harm and report immediately
Expect marked drowsiness, dizziness, and unsteadiness (ataxia), especially early - avoid driving or operating machinery until you know how it affects you
Do not stop the medication suddenly - abrupt withdrawal can trigger prolonged seizures (status epilepticus)
Avoid alcohol and other sedating substances
If you become pregnant, do not stop the drug; tell your clinician and enroll in the NAAED Pregnancy Registry (1-888-233-2334)
Nursing infants may become unusually sleepy - report this to your clinician
pk: Anticonvulsant effect develops gradually; full assessment of a regimen takes several weeks
Primidone peaks roughly 3 hours after an oral dose
Primidone ~5-15 hours; active metabolites longer (phenobarbital ~75-120 hours, PEMA ~16-25 hours)
Sustained by long-acting metabolites; given in divided doses (t.i.d.-q.i.d.)
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); dispense in a tight, light-resistant, child-resistant container
pearls: Class risk of suicidal thoughts/behavior with antiepileptics - monitor mood; marked sedation, especially early in therapy
Metabolized to two active anticonvulsants: phenobarbital and PEMA (phenylethylmalonamide)
Contraindicated in porphyria and in phenobarbital hypersensitivity
Early ataxia and vertigo often resolve with continued therapy or a lower starting dose
Never stop abruptly - risk of status epilepticus; the 250 mg tablet contains tartrazine
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered. If it is nearly time for the next dose, skip the missed one and resume the regular schedule - do not double up. Do not stop the medication on your own.
overdose: Overdose produces profound CNS and respiratory depression resembling barbiturate (phenobarbital) toxicity - deep sedation, coma, hypotension, and depressed reflexes. Management is supportive with airway protection and respiratory/circulatory support; consider measures to enhance elimination. There is no specific antidote.
